prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit.

We represent: plaintiff.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a plaintiff need not plead a prima facie case of discrimination to survive a Rule 12(b)(6) motion, but must allege facts supporting a plausible inference of discrimination.

Cite at least six decisions of the Fourth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### I. A Title VII Plaintiff Need Not Plead a Prima Facie Case; She Must Allege Facts That Plausibly Support an Inference of Discrimination.

#### A. The Rule 12(b)(6) standard is plausibility, not proof.

This Court reviews a Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal de novo, accepting the well-pleaded facts as true and drawing all reasonable inferences in the plaintiff's favor. *Wright v. North Carolina*, 787 F.3d 256, 263 (4th Cir. 2015); *Nemet Chevrolet, Ltd. v. Consumeraffairs.com, Inc.*, 591 F.3d 250, 255 (4th Cir. 2009). A complaint survives if it contains enough factual matter to state a claim that is plausible on its face. *Bell Atl. Corp. v. Twombly*, 550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007); *Ashcroft v. Iqbal*, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009). Plausibility does not demand probability, and the court may not weigh competing inferences or test the evidence. *Francis v. Giacomelli*, 588 F.3d 186, 192–93 (4th Cir. 2009).

#### B. The *McDonnell Douglas* prima facie case is an evidentiary framework, not a pleading requirement.

The Supreme Court has held that the prima facie case "is an evidentiary standard, not a pleading requirement." *Swierkiewicz v. Sorema N.A.*, 534 U.S. 506, 510 (2002). A discrimination plaintiff therefore need not plead each element of the prima facie case to survive a motion to dismiss. *Id.* at 510–12. *Twombly* did not disturb that rule. 550 U.S. at 569–70.

This Court has said the same repeatedly. In *Coleman v. Maryland Court of Appeals*, 626 F.3d 187, 190 (4th Cir. 2010), *aff'd*, 566 U.S. 30 (2012), the Court explained that *Swierkiewicz* remains good law and that a complaint need not set out facts establishing a prima facie case. *Accord Woods v. City of Greensboro*, 855 F.3d 639, 648 (4th Cir. 2017); *Bing v. Brivo Sys., LLC*, 959 F.3d 605, 616–17 (4th Cir. 2020). Instead, the plaintiff must allege facts that satisfy the elements of the cause of action the statute creates. *McCleary-Evans v. Md. Dep't of Transp., State Highway Admin.*, 780 F.3d 582, 584–85 (4th Cir. 2015); *Goode v. Cent. Va. Legal Aid Soc'y, Inc.*, 807 F.3d 619, 626 (4th Cir. 2015). The prima facie elements may inform that inquiry, but they do not set the pleading threshold. *See Woods*, 855 F.3d at 648.

#### C. The complaint must nonetheless allege facts, not conclusions, supporting a plausible inference of discrimination.

Eliminating the prima facie requirement does not excuse the plaintiff from pleading facts. In *McCleary-Evans*, the Court affirmed dismissal because the complaint offered only the conclusion that the decisionmakers acted because of the plaintiff's race and sex, without facts that would move that explanation from conceivable to plausible. 780 F.3d at 585–86. Labels and conclusions are not enough. *Francis*, 588 F.3d at 193. Thus, the question is whether the facts alleged, taken together and accepted as true, permit a reasonable inference that the adverse action occurred because of a protected characteristic. *Bing*, 959 F.3d at 617; *Woods*, 855 F.3d at 648–49.

A plaintiff may satisfy that burden through many kinds of facts, including more favorable treatment of similarly situated employees outside the protected class, discriminatory remarks, departures from ordinary procedure, or the circumstances and timing of the challenged decision. *See Coleman*, 626 F.3d at 190–91; *Bing*, 959 F.3d at 617–18. No single category is required.

#### D. Plaintiff's complaint satisfies that standard.

Plaintiff's complaint does not rest on a bare assertion that she was treated unfairly because of her protected status. It alleges specific facts: [describe protected status; qualifications; the adverse action; comparators or other circumstances supporting causation] (J.A. __). Accepted as true, those allegations identify who made the decision, what occurred, and why the circumstances point to a discriminatory motive. They therefore support a plausible inference of discrimination and distinguish this case from the conclusory pleading in *McCleary-Evans*. 780 F.3d at 585–86.

To the extent the district court faulted Plaintiff for failing to plead facts establishing each element of a *McDonnell Douglas* prima facie case, such as a similarly situated comparator, it applied the wrong standard. *See Swierkiewicz*, 534 U.S. at 510–12; *Woods*, 855 F.3d at 648; *Bing*, 959 F.3d at 616–17. Whether Plaintiff can ultimately prove her case under *McDonnell Douglas* is a question for summary judgment or trial, after discovery. At this stage, the only question is whether the complaint plausibly alleges discrimination, and it does. The dismissal should be reversed.
